{{Short description|Subcategory of welfare economics}}
{{Distinguish|Equity (economics)}}
[[File:US federal minimum wage if it had kept pace with productivity. Also, the inflation-adjusted minimum wage.png|thumb|upright=1.4|[[US federal minimum wage]] if it had kept pace with productivity compared to the real minimum wage]]
{{Taxation sidebar}}
'''Economic justice''' is generally [[distributive justice]] and [[equality of outcome]] and sometimes a component of [[social justice]] in a [[Normativity|normative]] sense, as several economic theories and approaches provide insights in understanding distributive justice.<ref name="Fleurbaey 2026">{{Cite encyclopedia |last=Fleurbaey |first=Marc |title=Normative Economics and Economic Justice |date=2026 |encyclopedia=The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy |editor-last=Zalta |editor-first=Edward N. |url=https://plato.stanford.edu/archives/sum2026/entries/economic-justice/ |access-date=2026-06-12 |edition=Summer 2026 |publisher=Metaphysics Research Lab, Stanford University |editor2-last=Nodelman |editor2-first=Uri}}</ref> Economic justice is the desired outcome of just and fair [[economic institution]]s, with the ultimate goal of providing a sufficient material foundation for a dignified, productive, and creative life.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Economic Justice |url=https://www.investopedia.com/terms/e/economic-justice.asp |access-date=2023-02-27 |website=Investopedia |language=en}}</ref> What is just and fair remains deeply contested, often along [[political affiliation]]s. [[Welfare economics]] traditionally is normative economics, generically speaking, and has since come to be associated with a particular subdomain in economics.<ref name="Fleurbaey 2026" />

Some ideas about justice and ethics overlap with the origins of economic thought,<ref>[[Joseph J. Spengler]], 1980. ''Origins of Economic Thought and Justice''. Link to 1-page chapter-content [https://www.questia.com/read/59213409 previews] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110810012211/http://www.questia.com/read/59213409 |date=2011-08-10 }}.</ref> often as to [[distributive justice]]<ref>

[https://web.archive.org/web/20061201121941/http://www.u-cergy.fr/IMG/2000-37.pdf "Is There Progress in Normative Economics?"], same title in Stephan Boehm et al., eds., 2002, ''Is There Progress in Economics?''.</ref> In early welfare economics, where it was mentioned, 'justice' was little distinguished from maximization of all individual [[utility|utility functions]] or a [[social welfare function]]. As to the latter, [[Paul Samuelson]] (1947),<ref>Paul A. Samuelson, 1947. ''[[Foundations of Economic Analysis]]'', ch. VIII ("Welfare Economics"), p. 221.</ref> expanding on the work of [[Abram Bergson]], [[representation (mathematics)|represents]] a social welfare function in general terms as any ethical belief system required to order any (hypothetically feasible) social states for the entire society as "better than", "worse than", or "indifferent to" each other. [[Kenneth Arrow]] (1963) showed a difficulty of trying to extend a social welfare function consistently across different hypothetical [[ordinal utility function]]s, even aside from considerations of justice.<ref>Kenneth J. Arrow, 1963. ''[[Social Choice and Individual Values]]'', 2nd ed.</ref> Utility maximization survives, even with the rise of [[ordinal utility|ordinal-utility]]/[[Pareto efficiency|Pareto]] theory, as an ethical basis for [[economic policy]] judgments<ref>

A broad reinterpretation of justice from the perspective of [[game theory]], [[social contract theory]], and [[evolutionary naturalism]] is found in the works of [[Ken Binmore]] (1994, 1998, 2004) and others, who have invoked arguments on [[Fair division|fairness]] as an aspect of justice to explain a wide range of [[Behavioral economics|behavioral]] and theoretical applications, supplementing earlier emphasis on [[economic efficiency]].<ref>Konow, 2003.</ref>
